items.title: Hackers Chain PHP2Shell and Linux Kernel Exploits to Gain Root Access on 25 Servers
items.summary: Hackers combined PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with a Linux kernel exploit to gain root access on 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a US government-affiliated environment. Dream researchers uncovered the campaign’s files on October 25, revealing a path from exposed firewall management interfaces to internal Active Directory services. According to Dream’s investigation, the list includes custom exploits, target lists, attack logs, and roughly 40 post-compromise scripts. The affected firewall vendor has been notified, but its name and vulnerable software versions remain withheld for security reasons. PHP2Shell Exploit Chain Gained Root The attack paired PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , with Fragnesia, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw tracked as CVE-2026-46300. Dream described the PHP2Shell code as a custom, nonpublic implementation tailored to the targeted firewall platform, rather than a copy of a known public exploit. PHP2Shell targeted PHP’s session.upload_progress feature within the firewall’s appweb management server. Through several stages, the attacker exhausted memory, leaked a memory address, and manipulated damaged memory structures to run commands as the restricted nobody user. Fragnesia then changed local authentication data, allowing the attacker to become root without a password. The full chain reportedly installed a root webshell in under 15 minutes. Although the final request connected both exploits, earlier requests prepared memory for execution. Cyber Security News previously covered PHP2Shell exploitation and the underlying flaws , providing context for this campaign. Using FOFA, the attacker identified about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls. Roughly 5,000 returned version information, and filtering by location and software version narrowed the list to 240 targets. The operation ultimately compromised 24 firewalls, leaving webshells on 22 without further recorded activity beyond that initial access. Two firewalls linked to a US government-affiliated organization received closer attention. Configuration data exposed internal systems and network details. After the first firewall crashed, the attacker compromised the second on October 24 and established a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding eight internal ports. Startup settings allowed the tunnel to survive reboots. At 11:35 UTC that day, the attacker used the same exploit chain through the tunnel against an internal firewall management server. This became the 25th compromised system and exposed centrally managed firewall settings and credentials. Attack Path From there, the attacker decrypted an LDAP service account password and listed Active Directory users and groups. Password spraying, backdoor account creation, and SAML signing key theft were attempted, but their success remains unknown. These limits matter when assessing Active Directory attack paths , rather than assuming full domain control. Recovered systems contained Claude Code and an aiscan setup configured with DeepSeek and Kimi. Chinese-language prompts and UTC+8 timestamps supported Dream’s assessment of possible Chinese links. However, researchers found no direct proof that AI wrote the exploits, established no named actor attribution, and did not describe the campaign as fully autonomous. Dream recommends deploying relevant patches under vendor guidance. The broader concern is stolen access: fixing the entry point does not establish whether credentials, webshells, or tunnels remain usable. Investigators must distinguish confirmed credential theft and directory access from the still unverified outcomes of the attacker’s later identity attacks. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Hackers Leak Records of 41,000 DHS Personnel, Exposing Undercover ICE Agents
items.summary: A leak of records covering more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has exposed contact details, work assignments, and links to sensitive operations, including undercover ICE work. Published on October 28, the archive reveals far more than a staff directory, offering a view of internal teams and reporting lines. Distributed Denial of Secrets released the collection under the name Icepick, crediting a group calling itself Department of Peace. Researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew built a search tool for the records. The nonprofit says the release supports public oversight, journalism, and requests for government records. DHS Data Leak According to reports, the records were last updated on August 19, 2026. They include names, email addresses, phone numbers, office locations, job titles, and supervisors. The files cover DHS and seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. CBP accounts for more than half of the records, while roughly 10,000 relate to ICE. About 6,200 cover US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 concern CISA. The collection represents about one seventh of the department’s workforce, not every DHS worker. The most sensitive details appear in more than 55,000 permission groups, which help control access to internal systems. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees in groups containing “CUC,” a term government court records link to certified undercover operations. Other groups reference wiretaps, phone data analysis, and surveillance tools. DDoSecrets says the information came from an Okta single sign-on service used by DHS. However, Reuters could not confirm that claim . Okta said its systems were secure and that it had no evidence its data or systems had been compromised. No confirmed entry method has been disclosed. That distinction matters. A claimed theft from an organization’s identity service does not establish a breach of the identity provider itself. Separate reporting on attacks targeting Okta identity systems shows how criminals can target customer accounts through phone calls and false help desk requests. There is no confirmed link between those methods and this incident. Reuters could not verify the entire archive. It matched details for six employees against other records and confirmed phone numbers and other information by calling three workers. Some entries matched public profiles, while others revealed internal structures or previously undisclosed operations. Names become more useful to attackers when paired with supervisors, duties, and phone numbers. Recorded Future expert Alexander Leslie told WIRED that such information could help adversaries identify vulnerable staff, build convincing impersonation attempts, or threaten investigations. Group membership, however, should not automatically be treated as proof of a person’s current assignment. Previous Okta support impersonation campaigns show why exposed contact details matter. Attackers have used fake support messages and login pages to steal account information and authentication codes. The DHS records could provide material for similarly tailored approaches. The disclosure follows ShinyHunters’ September claim of stealing FBI personnel data and an October lawsuit over a Defense Department breach affecting millions. These are separate incidents, with no established common cause. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: WatchGuard Discloses 7 Critical Firewall Flaws Allowing Remote Code Execution and Root-Level Attacks
items.summary: WatchGuard disclosed seven critical Fireware OS vulnerabilities in an October 27, 2026 advisory, affecting Firebox firewalls and potentially enabling remote code execution, root-level action injection, and memory corruption. They are part of a wider release that covers 18 security issues across Fireware OS and the Windows Mobile VPN with SSL client. The seven critical entries carry severity scores between 9.1 and 9.5. Other issues in the release could expose configuration secrets, allow file changes with root rights, hijack sessions, or disrupt firewall services. Risks vary by service, software version, and the access an attacker needs. The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-103594, scores 9.5 and involves a stack buffer overflow in WireGuard configuration that allows remote code execution . Its affected ranges cover Fireware OS 2026.2 through versions before 2026.4, and 12.12 through versions before 12.12.4. Two further flaws, CVE-2026-112709 and CVE-2026-112710, each score 9.2. Both involve heap buffer overflows in the Active Directory authentication service and allow remote code execution before authentication. WatchGuard Discloses Critical Firewall Flaws WatchGuard’s indexed advisory confirms that description for CVE-2026-112710. These bugs are notable because attackers do not need to complete a login before triggering the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-93857, also rated 9.2, affects the SIP proxy and allows remote code execution before authentication through a stack buffer overflow. CVE-2026-103593 scores 9.1 and affects the logging service, where another stack buffer overflow can allow remote code execution. The remaining critical issues affect FireCluster synchronization and Access Portal. CVE-2026-93865 scores 9.2 and involves missing authentication in the FireCluster sync daemon, allowing remote root action injection. Critical Flaws : CVE ID CVSS Component Vulnerability CVE-2026-103594 9.5 WireGuard Stack buffer overflow CVE-2026-112710 9.2 Active Directory service Heap buffer overflow CVE-2026-112709 9.2 Active Directory service Heap buffer overflow CVE-2026-93865 9.2 FireCluster daemon Missing authentication CVE-2026-93857 9.2 SIP proxy Stack buffer overflow CVE-2026-93866 9.2 Access Portal Integer overflow CVE-2026-103593 9.1 Logging service Stack buffer overflow CVE-2026-93866 carries the same score and involves an integer overflow before authentication in Access Portal that allows an out-of-bounds write. That description establishes memory corruption, not confirmed code execution. Two lower-scored entries also involve root-level access. CVE-2026-90464 lets an authenticated attacker modify arbitrary files as root because it lacks command validation. CVE-2026-93864 allows a local attacker to overwrite arbitrary files as root through a link-following flaw in firewalld. Earlier reporting on WatchGuard Firebox OS vulnerabilities covered separate authenticated code execution and file-write issues. Do not confuse those earlier flaws with this release. For most listed Fireware OS issues, the supplied advisory data identifies 2026.4 and 12.12.4 as fixed versions. Where applicable, T15 and T35 devices require 12.5.22. The Windows SSL VPN client credential-exposure issue is fixed in 2026.4. Previous coverage of an exploited WatchGuard zero-day concerns CVE-2025-14733 , not these newly listed flaws. It does not establish exploitation of this release. We could not retrieve full advisory pages during verification. Apart from the indexed confirmation noted above, the October disclosure details and patch versions therefore remain based on the supplied list and need confirmation before publication. items.title: Fortinet Brings AI Agent Security to Oracle Cloud to Block Prompt Injection and Data Leaks
items.summary: Fortinet’s FortiAIGate is bringing AI security controls to enterprise workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) , helping businesses inspect prompts, block sensitive data leaks, and control agent actions. An Oracle announcement published October 27 outlines how customers can combine the self-hosted gateway with OCI Enterprise AI to protect applications connected to company data and tools. The approach addresses a growing security gap as AI agents move beyond answering questions. Agents can query databases, access code, and call business tools. Monitoring chat messages alone leaves other interactions unchecked, including tool responses that could carry hidden instructions or expose private information. FortiAIGate runs as a containerized, GPU-powered reverse proxy between applications and AI models. It routes requests through security checks before they reach their destination. The gateway also inspects model responses, giving security teams a central place to apply rules across AI services. Fortinet Secures Oracle Cloud AI Agents Its Model Context Protocol (MCP) protection checks tool lists, calls, and responses in both directions. Fortinet says these checks detect prompt injection, data leaks, and harmful content in traffic between agents and MCP servers. FortiAIGate and OCI reference architecture (source : Fortinet ) This extends inspection beyond the user’s original request to the information agents receive while completing tasks. That threat has surfaced in research covered by Cybersecuritynews.com on prompt injection through malicious MCP servers . Researchers described how hidden instructions could redirect conversations or trigger tool use without clear user consent. Separate reporting on attacks targeting AI infrastructure detailed attempts to exploit exposed gateways and agent tools. According to Oracle, FortiAIGate uses Virtue AI guardrails to inspect prompts and responses across nine languages. Built-in data loss prevention detects 35 types of sensitive information and can block or redact matches. Administrators can also describe custom detection rules in plain language. Role-based workspaces separate team policies, model access, and logs while keeping central oversight. More than 50 preset policies cover privacy, security, and AI governance requirements. Workspace policy changes require approval, while records of routed prompts, outputs, and tool calls support audits. These features help enforce rules but do not establish compliance. The gateway also limits spending by organization, workspace, project, user, and virtual key. Requests stop when budgets run out. Rate limits restrict requests and tokens per minute. At the same time, guardrails target denial-of-wallet attacks designed to consume paid AI resources. Content-based routing can send routine work to cheaper models. The reference design places FortiAIGate on GPU-enabled Oracle Kubernetes Engine worker nodes. A hub-and-spoke setup can centralize inspection while applications operate across separate cloud networks. According to Fortinet , OCI Enterprise AI provides managed model access, agent tools, and governance. Self-hosting keeps gateway logs and inspection data within the customer’s environment, while model requests still reach the selected provider. Businesses must therefore check model routing and processing locations against their data residency needs. Protection also depends on sending relevant traffic through the gateway, rather than leaving alternate application paths outside inspection. items.title: WordPress 7.1.4 Fixes 22 Security Flaws, Including an Unauthenticated RCE Vulnerability
items.summary: WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28, 2026, fixing 22 security flaws, including an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in its update process. The security release also addresses stored cross-site scripting, data exposure, and access control issues. WordPress urges website owners to install the update immediately. The official release announcement credits security researcher Umut Bayram with reporting the update flaw. Patchstack’s technical analysis describes 22 vulnerabilities across 17 advisories, explaining why the number of listed advisory entries differs from the total flaw count. The release was led by Aaron Jorbin and Nik Tsekouras, with reports from independent researchers and the WordPress Security Team helping close weaknesses across older and newer features. The most serious issue involves a race condition, where an attacker must reach a temporary installation at precisely the right time. Exploitation requires no WordPress account, but the attack depends on a short update window and public access to the wp-content/upgrade/ directory. During updates, WordPress extracts files into that directory. Previously, predictable folder names and cleanup that removed index.php could expose an unpacked WordPress installer. An attacker reaching it during the update could run setup using a database they control, creating a path to code execution. WordPress 7.1.4 adds 16 random characters to temporary folder names, restores index.php protection, and prevents wp-config.php from being copied from the working directory. Patchstack rates exploitation as difficult because the opportunity lasts only seconds. This is separate from the earlier WordPress Core template resolution vulnerability covered by Cybersecuritynews.com. Stored XSS and Permission Gaps Several fixes target the Interactivity API, which supports interactive page features. Attackers with Contributor access could save crafted attributes that passed content filtering but later triggered unsafe browser actions. The update blocks dangerous bindings, strengthens checks, and addresses a denial-of-service issue that could freeze a visitor’s browser tab. Other stored XSS fixes cover crafted block markup, Customizer selective refresh, Categories, and navigation labels. Image and Playlist processing also received hardening. Stored XSS means harmful script content remains saved on a site and runs when another user opens the affected content. Anthropic reported issues involving personal data removal requests and specially crafted usernames. A separate Customizer flaw exposed unpublished changes to visitors without accounts. WordPress also tightened note permissions so users cannot access notes attached to posts they lack permission to edit. These changes follow earlier WordPress security updates addressing similar risks. Update WordPress and Check Protection Administrators can install the release through Dashboard, Updates, and Update Now, or download WordPress 7.1.4 directly. Sites with automatic background updates should receive it automatically, but owners should confirm the installed version rather than assume the process completed. The official version documentation lists patched older branches, including 7.0.8, 6.9.11, and releases extending to 4.7.39. Not every branch contains all 22 flaws. Only the latest WordPress version remains actively supported, while versions 4.6 and earlier receive no security updates. Beyond patching, Patchstack recommends blocking web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server and reviewing accounts with Contributor privileges or higher. A WordPress plugin firewall may not protect the extracted installer because that copy loads independently. The release also updates bundled root certificates following the eMudhra revocation. WordPress 7.2 remains scheduled for December 8, but site owners should not delay this security update while waiting for that major release. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #490: How Jared Kushner’s iPhone was allegedly hacked twice
items.summary: Dutch spies, Russian hackers and Jared Kushner’s iPhone. It sounds like the ingredients for a thriller, but according to claims in a new book the US President's son-in-law may have been hacked twice. Is any of it true, and what does it tell us about the phones in our pockets? Meanwhile, James Ball explains that of the internet’s most trusted security keys were protected by numbers so small that one of them was... four. Yes, "4". items.title: Offensivecon Tokyo 2026 Review
items.summary: This conference was an interesting experience for me, though probably not for the reasons I originally expected. There were some genuinely excellent presentations and valuable technical insights, but also some pretty disappointing moments that left me questioning whether attending was worth it. A few friends and I submitted talks back on June 1st, but acceptance decisions weren't announced until late September. For an international conference in Japan in late October, that meant committing to flights and travel arrangements before knowing whether we'd be presenting. None of our talks were accepted, but with our trips already booked, we decided to attend anyway, despite the additional $1,800 per person conference admission. At that price, especially when the talks are eventually released online for free, you're paying for an experience that should offer substantially more than just access to presentations. I was still optimistic going in, but after the opening keynote, I couldn't help feeling like I'd been sold something very different from what I'd expected. What had initially seemed like unfortunate travel logistics and an expensive ticket suddenly started to feel like a pretty questionable investment. I think keynote presentations carry a particular responsibility that ordinary conference talks don't. A keynote is often an attendee's first real impression of a conference. It establishes the tone, introduces the themes, and implicitly communicates what the organizers believe is important or representative of the event. In many ways, the opening keynote is the conference's opportunity to demonstrate why attendees should be excited about everything that follows. That's why the Day 1 keynote was especially disappointing. Based on the title, I was genuinely excited to hear a discussion of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), particularly given how rapidly AI is changing and how much interest there is in systems that can iteratively improve their own capabilities. This is an incredibly relevant topic for vulnerability research, where AI is already forcing us to reconsider many of our assumptions about how research gets performed. Instead, the presentation largely focused on extracting insights at minimal cost, building benchmarks, and constructing datasets. Those are perfectly legitimate subjects, but they weren't what I understood the talk to be promising. As far as I could tell, there wasn't an actual demonstration or particularly substantive discussion of recursive model self-improvement. I was also left wondering how XBOW's approach related to RSI in the traditional sense, particularly given my understanding that they rely on models they don't directly control. The entire presentation felt more like a loosely assembled vendor pitch than the carefully considered technical keynote I'd expected. And that's where the experience really started to sour for me. After spending thousands of dollars to travel internationally and attend, sitting through what felt like a promotional presentation as the opening keynote left me feeling like I'd paid for something very different from what I'd been led to expect. I don't think it's unreasonable to expect significantly more from the keynote of a conference charging this much money. A keynote isn't just another presentation in the schedule; it sets expectations for the quality, direction, and substance of the entire event. When it misses that mark so dramatically, it affects how you perceive everything that comes afterward. The physical conference itself also caught me off guard. The entire event was essentially contained within a single conference room and an adjoining hallway, with one vendor, XBOW, and perhaps five to seven tables for eating or socializing. There was very little space outside the main room for people to congregate. During a coffee break on the second day, I tried counting attendees and came up with somewhere around 60 people. Now, there's nothing inherently wrong with a small conference. Some of the best technical exchanges happen at smaller, more focused events. But the combination of the scale, facilities, and exceptionally high ticket price was difficult to reconcile. There was also a noticeable sense that many attendees and speakers already knew one another from previous offensive security conferences or shared professional backgrounds. It seemed like quite a few had worked together at places like Binary Gecko, XBOW, or elsewhere in the industry. Again, that's not necessarily a bad thing. Tight-knit research communities are common, especially in offensive security. But as someone attending from outside those established circles, I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd somehow paid a substantial amount of money to attend what was, in practice, a relatively small gathering of people who already knew one another. Despite all of this, I don't want to dismiss the entire conference, because there were genuinely good presentations. The Day 2 keynote, in particular, was a substantial improvement. It addressed something I think is critically important right now, the fact that our industry is changing rapidly, and that researchers and organizations will need to adapt if they want to remain relevant. I didn't agree with every technical detail, particularly some of the discussion around influencing training data and exploiting that material, but the broader message resonated with me. Several other talks also stood out, either because they were exceptionally well presented and showed some various novel components on how to infer or understand data with vulnerability research. Those presentations provided real value. They offered interesting technical insights, introduced new ideas, and gave me things to think about afterward. They were the moments when the conference began to resemble what I'd originally hoped it would be. But they also highlighted something else that I found increasingly difficult to ignore. We're in the middle of what feels like a software industrial revolution. AI is fundamentally changing how we write, understand, analyze, and interact with software. The implications go far beyond simply making individual researchers more productive. We're starting to see changes in the economics and scale of vulnerability discovery, the automation of complex analysis, and the processes through which entire software systems are developed and secured. Vulnerability research is right in the middle of that transformation. And yet, what surprised me most was how little of that transformation seemed to be reflected in the overall direction of the conference. Almost everyone seemed aware of what was happening. Many presenters were already using AI in their research, and conversations throughout the event made it clear that researchers understood the significance of these tools. But much of the selected content still seemed anchored in the traditional model of vulnerability research: finding highly specific bugs, developing intricate exploitation techniques, and presenting the technical details of individual discoveries. There's obviously still tremendous value in that work. Deep technical understanding and exploitation expertise aren't suddenly irrelevant just because AI is getting better. But the methods by which we discover, analyze, and ultimately exploit vulnerabilities are changing underneath us. I would have loved to see more discussion of that shift. Not simply talks about using an LLM to assist with an existing workflow, but serious exploration of what vulnerability research looks like when the fundamental constraints around time, scale, cost, and human effort start to change. It felt like the community understood that a major transformation was underway, while the conference's overall program was still largely organized around the world that existed before it. Perhaps that's just the nature of a conference with a particular technical focus. But I couldn't help wondering whether the talk selection reflected a disconnect between where the industry has traditionally placed its attention and where the most consequential developments are now happening. I came away with mixed feelings. There were undeniably talented researchers at this event, and some of the presentations were excellent. I learned things, heard interesting perspectives, and had conversations that made attending worthwhile. But I also came away feeling that the overall experience didn't remotely justify its cost. And I keep coming back to that keynote. When you're asking people to spend thousands of dollars, often traveling across the world to attend, your opening presentation should make them feel confident that they've made a worthwhile investment. It should represent the intellectual ambition and technical quality of the event. Instead, I spent much of that first morning wondering why I'd paid so much money to listen to what felt like a sales pitch. The stronger presentations that followed helped recover some of that initial disappointment, but they couldn't entirely erase it. I'm genuinely curious to see how this conference evolves as AI continues to reshape vulnerability research and the broader software industry. There's certainly an opportunity for it to become a place where researchers grapple with some of the most important changes happening in our field. For now, though, I suspect I'll be following that evolution from the sidelines, watching the presentations online rather than paying to attend in person again.
